episode_title: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek

stories.topic: Why Amit's Dog Is Named Freddie
stories.summary: Amit's dog Freddie is named after his two intellectual heroes — Frederic Bastiat and Friedrich Hayek, both Freddies. The episode is built around these two thinkers, with the dog sitting in the frame throughout. Amit even riffs that Milton Friedman, with a twist of the name, could be a third Freddy.
stories.insight: A small, warming detail that reveals how deeply ideas can shape an intellectual life — even your pet's name carries the lineage of the thinkers who formed your worldview.

stories.summary: Frederic Bastiat died at 49 — the same age as Amit — having travelled France popularising his ideas and contracting tuberculosis in the process. As his lungs weakened and he knew the end was near, he wrote: 'Until the day of my death I shall proclaim principle with all the force of my lungs, which alas is all too inadequate.' Joseph Schumpeter called him 'the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived.'
stories.insight: A reminder that ideas can be worth dying for, and that the man who first popularised opportunity cost did so before the term even existed. The poignancy is also about loss — what could he have written in another fifty years?

stories.topic: The Bastiat Prize Trophy Is a Candlestick
stories.summary: Amit was the first person ever to win the Bastiat Prize twice (Tim Harford has since matched this). The trophy is a candlestick — a wink at Bastiat's most famous satire, the Candlemakers' Petition. Amit is not one for material goods, but those two candlesticks are among his most prized possessions.
stories.insight: A nice instance of an award that lives up to its namesake's spirit — the trophy itself encodes the joke. The candlestick is the artifact through which Bastiat's argument is silently passed forward.

stories.summary: As a student in 1993-94, Amit volunteered after the Gujarat earthquake, riding into a flattened village in an ambulance with paramedics. Most buildings had collapsed, but a couple of shops were open and had tripled or quadrupled the price of bread. Amit's first thought was 'this is evil.' Later he realised: without the price hike, the first family in line would have bought all the bread. Higher prices forced families to pool resources and share, so everyone got a couple of slices.
stories.insight: Moral intuition and economic intuition often pull in opposite directions in a crisis. 'Price gouging' looks evil but functions as triage — it rations a scarce resource by intensity of need. Cheap bread by fiat means the first comer hoards; expensive bread by market means everyone eats.

stories.topic: The Friend Who Missed His Flight Because of an Uber Price Cap
stories.summary: About three years before the recording, the Delhi government experimented with capping Uber surge pricing. Amit's friend, the day after the cap came in, could not find a cab to the airport at any price and missed his flight. The cap, designed to protect consumers, instantly produced the shortage that price would have prevented.
stories.insight: Vivid, concrete demonstration that price controls do not abolish scarcity — they just hide it as queues, waits, missed flights and (in the case of stents) deaths. The casualty of a populist price cap is often the very person it was meant to help.

stories.topic: Tweeting That Stent Price Controls Would Kill
stories.summary: When the Indian government imposed a price cap on cardiac stents to make them affordable, Amit tweeted (and wrote a column) predicting shortages and deaths. Exactly that happened — the cheaper stents disappeared, suppliers exited, patients suffered. He uses this as a real-world receipt for the abstract law that price controls always create shortages.
stories.insight: A clear case where economic literacy is not academic — it is forecasting power. The mechanism (capped prices below market clearing → reduced supply → shortage) was predictable in advance, so the deaths were too. Good first principles let you see the future.

stories.summary: Ajay holds up Bezos taking on Trump as a striking proof-of-concept that institutions can work. Bezos, the world's richest man, owned the Washington Post; the Post pursued investigative journalism on Trump; the federal government and the office of the president were unable to shut it down or hit back at Bezos. The opposite case is Russia, where a billionaire newspaper owner in Putin's crosshairs 'experiences accidents — falls out of a window.'
stories.insight: Freedom is not the gift of any particular leader's good intentions — it is the residue of strong institutions. The test of a free society is whether private wealth can credibly stand up to the state. Where it cannot (Russia, increasingly China), 'oligarch' is just a courtesy title for a hostage.

stories.topic: Raj Narayan Suing Indira Over Government Jeeps
stories.summary: Ajay holds up a small Indian moment of institutional pride: in 1975, Raj Narayan dragged Indira Gandhi to Justice Sinha's courtroom in the Allahabad High Court for the 'sweet little problem' of using government jeeps for campaigning. The Congress party and the government of India were two distinct things, and using the second's jeeps for the first's purposes invalidated her election.
stories.insight: A reminder of what a healthy state looks like when constitutional niceties are honoured — the line between party and state is real, and even a sitting Prime Minister can be held to it. Such a prosecution would be unimaginable in Xi's China or Putin's Russia.

stories.topic: The Most Important Human of the Last 30 Years
stories.summary: Ajay sometimes asks people: who has had the greatest positive impact on humanity in the last 30 years? His own top candidate is Jeff Bezos. A friend countered with Deng Xiaoping — for lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. Amit, asked the same question, answers Ken Thompson, the main inventor of Unix.
stories.insight: The question is a thought-experiment that reveals values: Bezos (logistics and consumer surplus), Deng (mass material uplift), Thompson (the silent infrastructure of computation). What you choose betrays what you most prize about civilisation.

recommendations.item: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: Bastiat's foundational essay containing the parable of the broken window — and the namesake of Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen.
recommendations.reason: The single best onboarding text for the seen-vs-unseen frame: every action has visible immediate effects and invisible second-order ones, and the bad economist sees only the first. Free online; the rest of economic literacy can grow from this seed.

recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: Bastiat's short treatise on the proper role of law and the state.
recommendations.reason: Distinguishes property (wealth made by the perpetual application of one's faculties to objects) from plunder (seizing the productions of one's fellow men), and argues that most government interventions are subtle plunder. Amit: 'Every paragraph seems to contain such wisdom and such power and you're like, this guy lived in the nineteenth century, my God.'

recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: Bastiat's collection of satirical essays demolishing common economic fallacies, including the Candlemakers' Petition and the negative-railroad argument.
recommendations.reason: Bastiat's genius was distilling complex ideas into stories anyone could understand. Reductio ad absurdum done at a master level — once you've seen 'block out the sun to protect candlemakers' or 'ban the right hand to maximise productive effort,' you cannot un-see the absurdity in real protectionist arguments.

recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: Bastiat's satirical petition from candle-makers asking the French government to block out the sun, which is offering 'unfair competition' by giving free light.
recommendations.reason: The cleanest illustration of how the protectionist's logic, taken seriously, leads straight to absurdity. Also the joke encoded in the Bastiat Prize trophy — a candlestick.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's 1945 essay arguing that the price system is how dispersed knowledge across society gets used — written in response to Oscar Lange's case for a central price committee.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it the most important and seminal essay of the twentieth century. The core claim: knowledge is not concentrated anywhere; it is distributed across millions of heads, and only the price system can aggregate it. Any committee that tries to do the same will get it wrong, no matter how brilliant.

recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's late argument against the assumption that society can be planned by reason.
recommendations.reason: Sharpens the case made in 'The Use of Knowledge in Society': information is dispersed, the central planner cannot ever know enough, and the conceit that they can is fatal. Especially relevant now that the computer revolution has tempted people to believe centralisation might finally be tractable — Ajay frames the AI/Big Data central-planning fantasy as the same whack-a-mole returning.

recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: A first-person account by an ordinary pencil of how it came to exist — graphite from one country, wood from another, brass, rubber, paint, lacquer from forty-odd more.
recommendations.reason: The cleanest illustration of spontaneous order ever written. Nobody coordinates the people who make a pencil; they have never met and do not share a language. The price system is their language, and it produces the pencil — and the iPhone — without any central planner. Amit refers to it as 'magical.'

recommendations.context: A short film adaptation of Leonard Read's essay.
recommendations.reason: The visual, animated rendering of Read's parable for those who learn better by watching than reading.

recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Ridley's wide-ranging argument that order in cities, languages, technologies, morals and economies is mostly bottom-up emergence rather than top-down design.
recommendations.reason: Generalises spontaneous order beyond markets into culture, science and biology. Pairs naturally with Bastiat–Hayek by showing that the design-without-a-designer pattern is the deep structure of how the world organises itself.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Amit's early Seen and the Unseen episode with Matt Ridley.
recommendations.reason: The long-form companion to Ridley's book — a deep tour of spontaneous order across domains.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Dawkins' classic on natural selection, framed against the watchmaker argument for design.
recommendations.reason: The biological analogue of Hayek and Read: the eye is more wonderful than any wristwatch, yet has no designer. Reinforces that magnificent complex order can — indeed must — emerge without a central planner. Amit also notes Dennett and Pinker as adjacent reading.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Friedman's foundational case for the inseparability of economic and political freedom.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's sole pick of the episode. 'Each of the chapters was like an earthquake — it just shakes you and makes you think about the world.' Not introductory, but deep and powerful.

recommendations.creator: Milton and Rose Friedman
recommendations.context: Companion volume to Capitalism and Freedom; also a 16-episode TV series in the same spirit.
recommendations.reason: More accessible than Capitalism and Freedom and pairs well with it. Ties capitalism to consent: voluntary exchange, double thank-you moments, the difference between markets and cronyism.

recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: A 1946 popular-economics classic explicitly modelled on Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen frame.
recommendations.reason: Amit's headline recommendation. Hazlitt walks through tariffs, price controls, monetary inflation and other modern policy questions and shows how the same first principles dispatch each. Over a million copies in 40-plus languages. Anyone who reads it knows enough to see through most political economic arguments — and Amit recounts an economist sneering 'too many people who've only read Hazlitt are arguing with me' as itself a tell that Hazlitt is doing the job.

recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: A short, accessible introduction to Hayek's thought.
recommendations.reason: Recommended as the on-ramp because Hayek himself can be heavy going. Amit had recommended it in an earlier episode and brings it back here as the friendly entry point.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column laying out the central claim of the episode — that most government interventions redistribute from the poor to the rich.
recommendations.reason: The written companion to the teddy-bear-tariff example. The redistribution is real, just disguised by the rhetoric of protection.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column laying out the law that capped prices always produce shortages.
recommendations.reason: The written form of the stent and Uber arguments — used to make the case in advance that price controls would kill, before they did.

recommendations.item: Why Both Modi and Trump are Textbook Populists
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column defining populism via Jan-Werner Muller's framework and applying it.
recommendations.reason: Populism, Amit argues, is most distinctively a politics of simplistic narratives — 'foreigners are taking your jobs,' 'China is shipping your jobs overseas.' These slogans are emotionally potent precisely because the truth is multifactorial and impossible to put on a placard.

recommendations.creator: Jan-Werner Muller
recommendations.context: Muller's short, definitional book on populism as a political style.
recommendations.reason: The framework Amit's populism column draws on: populism as the claim that 'we, and only we, represent the real people.' Pairs with the broader episode argument that populists trade in simple-minded economics.

recommendations.creator: Elias Canetti
recommendations.context: Canetti's grand study of how crowds form, behave, and become instruments of power.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's recommended companion to thinking about why simplistic economic narratives win — they mobilise crowds. Connects the seen-and-unseen problem to the political economy of rage.

recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Stossel's short piece on the moment in voluntary exchange when both buyer and seller say 'thank you.'
recommendations.reason: The cleanest possible refutation of the zero-sum view of trade. If both parties thank each other, both are better off — capitalism, properly understood, is consent.

recommendations.item: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive into what GDP measures and what it doesn't.
recommendations.reason: Background to Amit's gripe that government spending is counted in GDP — opening the door to the 'dig ditches and fill them in' style of growth that adds to the number while making nobody better off.

recommendations.item: Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek
recommendations.creator: EconStories (John Papola and Russ Roberts)
recommendations.context: An economics rap battle between Keynes and Hayek, dramatising their debate.
recommendations.reason: A fun, viral way into the Keynes-Hayek debate that the show treats as basically settled in Hayek's favour by the end of the 20th century.

recommendations.item: Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek Round Two
recommendations.creator: EconStories (John Papola and Russ Roberts)
recommendations.context: Sequel to the Keynes vs. Hayek rap battle.
recommendations.reason: The follow-up round, equally accessible and useful for new converts to the price-system view.

core_ideas.explanation: Bastiat's central frame: every action has a visible, immediate effect (the seen) and a set of invisible, downstream consequences (the unseen). The broken window appears to stimulate the economy because the glazier earns; what is unseen is the suit or cake the homeowner would otherwise have bought, and the work that money would have funded. The bad economist looks only at the first-order effect; the good economist follows the consequences out. The frame applies to war, GDP, tariffs, price controls — almost every policy.
core_ideas.quote: A bad economist will only look at your first-order effect. But a good economist will take everything into account.

core_ideas.explanation: Robert K. Merton's 1936 idea: all purposive social action has unintended consequences. The world is complex, nonlinear, and only dimly understood; even when we look hard, deeper effects surprise us. Pair this with the seen-and-unseen frame and you get a doubled humility — the unseen is sometimes hidden in plain sight, and sometimes genuinely beyond what anyone can foresee.

core_ideas.concept: Conspiracy Theories Are the Opiate of the Masses (Popper)
core_ideas.explanation: Karl Popper's twist: because the world is so complex and cause-and-effect so nonlinear, coordinating twenty people to pull off a complicated secret plan is nearly impossible — the ball would have to meander through three streams to find a hole far away. So most conspiracy theories beggar belief. To accept one is to mistake the world for something simpler than it is.
core_ideas.quote: Conspiracy theories are the opiate of the masses.

core_ideas.explanation: Populists win by replacing multifactorial truths with appealing two-line stories. Trump 2016: 'China stole your jobs' and 'Mexicans took your jobs' — partly true, mostly false, but slogan-shaped. Real explanations are too complex for a placard. The same dynamic mobilises 'protect local jobs' politics around the world. The seen-and-unseen problem becomes catastrophic in democracy because the seen narrative is easy to chant.

A core public choice insight. A tariff makes a teddy bear ten rupees more expensive: each consumer barely notices the loss, but the local manufacturer and lobbying group reap the entire concentrated gain. Because the losers are unorganised and unaware while the winners are organised and motivated, bad policies are politically rational even when they are economically destructive — and they redistribute from the (many, poor) consumers to the (few, rich) protected producers.

core_ideas.concept: Most Interventions Redistribute From the Poor to the Rich
core_ideas.explanation: The episode's claim 'in capital letters.' Tariffs, price controls, licensing, and subsidies are typically dressed up as protection of the poor or the worker; in practice they shrink the consumer's purchasing power, transfer it to a politically connected lobby, and remove the incentive for the protected business to improve. The intention is great; the redistribution runs in the opposite direction.
core_ideas.quote: Most government interventions in the economy, if not all, redistribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.concept: Tariffs Beat Blowing Up the Railroad — Because of Discretion
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's public-choice elaboration on Bastiat's negative-railroad satire. Blowing up a railway and imposing a tariff have similar economic effects on consumers, but the tariff is strictly better for the state — because the tariff is discretionary. It can be raised, lowered, granted to one industry, denied to another. That discretion creates a Sword of Damocles over the bourgeoisie. The state isn't just redistributing; it's preserving godlike power over the entrepreneurial class.
core_ideas.quote: What is one thing better than redistributing from the poor to the rich? The answer is achieving godlike power over the entrepreneurial class to boot.

core_ideas.explanation: Bastiat's dichotomy: man can build wealth by applying his faculties to objects (property) or by seizing the productions of his fellow men (plunder). Modern plunder is rarely direct theft — it is the use of state coercion to extract via tariffs, regulation, licensing, and rent-seeking. People will choose whichever is less burdensome. When honest commerce is hard, plunder is rational; this is how cronyism becomes the default career path in over-regulated economies.

Ajay's modern reformulation of Bastiat. Makers innovate, build, serve consumers and grow firms; takers organise the state to grab what makers have built. When the state has a monopoly on violence, takers route their grabs through it — regulations, licences, board seats, princeling protection. China is the textbook case: every significant business now has Communist Party members on its board or shares pledged to a princeling. 'A government that will give you anything you want is a government that can take away everything that you have.'
core_ideas.quote: Every form of refuge has a price.

core_ideas.concept: The Price System as Information, Incentive, and Coordination
core_ideas.explanation: Hayek's central insight: the price system is not just a settlement mechanism, it is a communication network. A high Uber surge price (a) tells the rider that cabs are scarce, (b) gives an idle driver an incentive to come online, and (c) coordinates the meeting between them with no central planner involved. Take prices away (price controls) and you blind the system. The first 20 cabs go to the first 20 callers regardless of need; the person rushing to hospital is left stranded while the casual mall-goer rides.
core_ideas.quote: We don't need to know each other. We don't need to talk to each other. We just look at the prices and everything happens.

core_ideas.explanation: When the cap is below the market-clearing price, supply contracts and demand swells; the gap shows up as shortage, queues, black markets, and missed flights. The Indian stent cap killed people. The Delhi Uber cap caused missed flights. The mechanism is universal — for cars, for housing, for vaccines, for stents. 'You cannot legislate scarcity away.'

core_ideas.concept: Spontaneous Order / Self-Organising Systems / Discovery, Not Design
core_ideas.explanation: Adam Ferguson's phrase: things which are 'the product of human action but not human design.' Languages, cities, markets, ecosystems are not planned — they emerge from millions of local decisions and mutual coordination. Ajay prefers the more technical term 'self-organising system,' borrowed from mathematics. Both express the same truth: the world is best run as a centralised process of discovery, not a centralised process of design.

Hayek's argument against central planning. The relevant information about wants, capacities, costs, and conditions is dispersed across millions of heads — your need for an airport cab, the driver's willingness to leave lunch and earn. No central planner can ever know all of it. So planners always get it wrong, not for lack of will but for lack of access. The price system, by contrast, aggregates the information automatically.

core_ideas.concept: The Fatal Conceit and Adam Smith's Man of System
core_ideas.explanation: Adam Smith's 'man of system' imagines society as a chess board on which he can move pieces freely; Hayek calls the same urge the fatal conceit. The 20th-century verdict was clear: central planning produces stagnation, because innovation comes from people pursuing their own values with local knowledge, not from bureaucrats. Yet the computer revolution keeps reigniting the fantasy — 'with enough data and AI, surely now we can plan everything.' Ajay calls this whack-a-mole: it pops up, you beat it down, it pops up again.

core_ideas.concept: We Are All AGIs Walking the Planet
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's reframe of Hayek for the AI age: each human being is already 'a clever, sentient, ambitious creature pursuing their own values' — an autonomous general intelligence operating on local information. The market economy is the discovery process they self-organise into. The error of the central planner is to treat humans as inputs to a plan rather than as the planning units themselves.

Amit's alliterative reframe. Capitalism is not greed; it is the voluntary action of people making each other better off. The 'double thank-you moment' (Stossel) — buyer and seller both saying thank you at the moment of exchange — is the everyday signature of a positive-sum relationship. People often conflate capitalism with cronyism, but cronies collude while markets compete: what is good for big business is often bad for the market, and vice versa.
core_ideas.quote: If you're for consent, you're for capitalism.

core_ideas.explanation: The Bezos vs. Trump anecdote crystallises this. The President of the United States, the most powerful office on earth, could not silence the Washington Post or punish its owner. In Russia, billionaires fall out of windows. The difference is not that America has nicer leaders — it is that the institutional machinery (independent judiciary, free press, separation of powers, rule of law) actually constrains the executive. Strong institutions, not good intentions, are what protect freedom.

core_ideas.concept: The Maslow of Civilisation: Safety and Freedom Before Prosperity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's response to the Deng case: even granting that hundreds of millions came out of poverty in China, the first-order question is whether people have safety and freedom — and most Chinese people, arguably, do not. Putin's Russia is a cautionary preview of how reversible material gains are when the underlying institutional order is brittle. Amit pushes back: economic prosperity is itself a precondition for safety. The disagreement is itself useful — the frame is a hierarchy, but the ordering is debatable.

Bastiat's satire of work-quantity-as-productivity (the 'ban the right hand' petition): if doing more work were what made us better off, the way to maximise welfare would be to make work as hard as possible. The fallacy is real — modern policies often equate jobs created with prosperity, ignoring that productivity (output per unit input) is what actually grows wealth.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit reveals that his dog Freddie is named after the two Freddies — Frederic Bastiat and Friedrich Hayek. He keeps making sure the dog stays in the camera frame throughout. Late in the episode he riffs that Milton Friedman, with a twist of the name, could be a third Freddy.

Vartika's t-shirt-worthy line about the town of Karjat where they're recording: 'Badi Badi Baatein, Vada Pav Khaate' — 'big big talk, eating vada pav.' Amit finds it perfectly targeted at the show. The joke doubles as the show's self-aware framing — intellectuals trading grand theories over street food.
Bastiat's reductio: 'destroy the railroad to protect local producers.' Once you laugh at the absurdity of the suggestion, you have to laugh at the underlying tariff policy too.

Bastiat's Candlemakers' Petition asks the French government to block out the sun, which is offering 'unfair competition' by giving free light to consumers. The trophy of the Bastiat Prize is, accordingly, a candlestick.
Bastiat's other satirical petition: ban everyone from working with their right hand. If quantity of work is what makes us prosperous, surely making work harder makes us richer.
Amit on the easiest way to grow GDP: have the government tax citizens and pay them to dig ditches and fill them back in. The number rises forever; nobody is better off.

Amit's flirty aside to Ajay on Hamlet/Ophelia coordination: 'If you ever play Ophelia, I will be happy to play Hamlet. But don't blush.' Sparked by Ajay's example of coordination — 'a bunch of people coming together: you'll play Hamlet and I'll play Ophelia' — to illustrate that prices spare us all that explicit negotiation.
Amit's parting line: liking and subscribing is itself a 'double thank you moment' — voluntary action, mutual benefit. 'It's a voluntary action. Double-thank-you more.'
Joseph Schumpeter on Bastiat: 'the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived.'
Adam Ferguson's phrase, quoted by Amit: societies and markets are 'the product of human action but not human design.' The Enlightenment-era origin of what economists now call spontaneous order.

Adam Smith's 'man of system' — the planner who imagines society as a chessboard he can rearrange at will. Used here as the antecedent of Hayek's fatal conceit and of every modern AI-empowered would-be central planner.
Jagdish Bhagwati's epigram, recalled by Amit: 'The Chinese are turning out to be profit-seeking while Indians are rent-seeking.'
Karl Popper on conspiracy theories: because cause-and-effect is nonlinear, coordinated secret plans almost never work. 'Conspiracy theories are the opiate of the masses.'
Robert K. Merton's 1936 'law of unintended consequences' — all purposive social action has unintended consequences.

Raj Narayan vs. Indira Gandhi, 1975 — invalidating a sitting Prime Minister's election over the use of government jeeps in campaigning. Held up as proof that, at its best, India honoured the line between party and state.
Russian oligarchs 'falling out of windows' — Ajay's shorthand for what happens to wealthy critics of Putin.
Ken Thompson — co-inventor of Unix. Amit's pick for the human with the greatest positive impact on the last 30 years.
'We didn't start the fire' — Amit's brief Billy Joel allusion when invoking Ken Thompson.
Daniel Pipes' Property and Freedom — referenced from a previous episode for the line that the freedom and flexibility of the rich is the test of whether a society is genuinely free.
Magna Carta as the dividing line in political history — before it, the king had unlimited, uncodified power to demand things; modern China and Russia operate, in effect, in that pre-Magna-Carta mode.
